Well, I... I came in because, well, it’s been going on for a while now, and I just can't shake it, no matter how much I try to rationalize it. I work as a personal financial advisor, right? And I have a lot of clients, a lot of connections, especially in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. It’s a tight-knit group, you know, everyone knows everyone, or at least they know of everyone. But lately, or I guess for a few months now, I’ve been absolutely convinced that certain people—specific people in these circles—are quietly tracking me. And it’s not just that they’re watching, it’s how they’re doing it. They’re sending me these... little signals. It sounds crazy when I say it out loud, but it’s in the details. Like, I’ll get an invitation to a gallery opening or a networking dinner, and the wording on the invite, or the specific panel topics they choose to discuss—it’s too specific to what I’ve been working on. And then at these events, it’s who sits near me. It’s always someone connected to a deal I’m looking at or a client I just met with. I keep telling myself, "Come on, it’s just a coincidence, Cincinnati isn't that big, it’s just how networking works." I try to brush it off. But I can’t. I just can’t let it go. It’s like this constant hum in the back of my mind, analyzing every interaction, every seating arrangement, every email subject line. Well, that's... that's the thing, isn't it? I mean, part of my brain, the logical part, the part that went to college and analyzes market trends and risk portfolios all day, that part says, "Hey, Cincinnati isn't New York, right? It's a smaller pond. You're going to see the same fish." And I really do try to lean into that. I'll sit there at my desk, looking at an email invite to a gallery opening in Over-the-Rhine, and I'll see that the featured artist just happens to be doing a series on, I don't know, urban decay, which exactly mirrors a real estate development deal I was just discussing in private with a client the day before. And I'll say to myself, "It's just a coincidence. It's just the zeitgeist." 

But then... I go to the event. And the person they seat next to me at the dinner afterward is the lead investor on a competing project. And the centerpieces are arranged in a way that... well, it just feels too deliberate. So, do I believe it for certain? I don't want to. I really, really don't want to. I try to talk myself out of it constantly. But the feeling, the absolute conviction that they are keeping tabs on me, that they are coordinating these little signals to let me know they're watching my moves... it just overpowers the logic. I can't shake it. No matter how much I tell myself it's crazy, I'm still absolutely convinced it's happening. It's like a weight I can't put down, just constantly analyzing the overlap, the connections, the sheer impossibility of it all being random chance. So, yes, despite my best efforts to rationalize it away, I am convinced they are tracking me.

Well, that’s... I mean, I really want it to be the first one. I really, really want it to just be my brain playing tricks on me, like some sort of weird stress response. I’d have a private consultation on a Tuesday about, say, tax-free municipal bonds, and by Thursday, someone at a downtown mixer would make a highly specific, pointed comment about that exact same financial vehicle while looking right at me. 

So it’s been two solid months of this. Sixty days of constantly analyzing the overlap. Well, no, I wouldn't call it sudden. And honestly, it wasn't really a stressful event that kicked it all off, either. I mean, not in a negative way, at least. I'll sit there at my desk, looking at an email invite to a gallery opening in Over-the-Rhine, and I'll see that the featured artist just happens to be doing a series on, I don't know, urban decay, which exactly mirrors a real estate development deal I was just discussing in private with a client the day before. And I'll say to myself, \"It's just a coincidence. It's just the zeitgeist.\" \n\nBut then... I go to the event. And the person they seat next to me at the dinner afterward is the lead investor on a competing project. And the centerpieces are arranged in a way that... well, it just feels too deliberate. So, do I believe it for certain? I don't want to. I really, really don't want to. I try to talk myself out of it constantly. But the feeling, the absolute conviction that they are keeping tabs on me, that they are coordinating these little signals to let me know they're watching my moves... it just overpowers the logic. I can't shake it. No matter how much I tell myself it's crazy, I'm still absolutely convinced it's happening. It's like a weight I can't put down, just constantly analyzing the overlap, the connections, the sheer impossibility of it all being random chance. So, yes, despite my best efforts to rationalize it away, I am convinced they are tracking me.\n\nDoctor: Have you heard voices when no one else was there?\n\nPatient: Voices? No, no, I haven't... it's not like that. I mean, my apartment is actually pretty quiet. I live alone in this loft over in the Pendleton area, and, you know, you get the standard city noise—sirens, delivery trucks, maybe some people walking back from the bars late at night—but I'm not hearing anyone talking to me in the room when it's empty. It’s nothing like that. \n\nMy internal monologue is just me. Just my own voice, you know, constantly running through client portfolios, trying to crunch the numbers, or... or trying to figure out the angles of why someone sent me a specific email or arranged a meeting a certain way. The signals I was talking about, the networking things, those are all things I can point to on paper or in a room. So, no, no voices or anything like that.\n\nDoctor: Do these thoughts about people tracking you feel intrusive and unwanted, like thoughts you know are probably not true but can’t stop, or do they feel like a real fact about what’s happening?\n\nPatient: Well, that’s... I mean, I really want it to be the first one. I really, really want it to just be my brain playing tricks on me, like some sort of weird stress response. Because in my line of work—being a financial advisor—you are literally trained to look for patterns, right? You look at market indicators, you analyze historical data, and you project forward. It’s all about finding the signal in the noise. You're just stressed about your portfolio.\" But... the problem is, it doesn't stay in my head. It doesn't feel like just a thought, because the evidence is physical. It feels like I've stumbled onto this coordinated effort to keep tabs on me. It becomes the reality you have to navigate every single day. I just keep trying to explain it away to myself, and I just end up right back at the absolute fact that it is actually happening.\n\nDoctor: About how long have you been convinced that these people are tracking you?\n\nPatient: Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... I actually went through my planner the other night trying to pinpoint the exact start of all this. Because, like I said, I'm an analytical guy. I need timelines, I need data points. And if I look at when the pattern really emerged, when I first became absolutely certain that this wasn't just some statistical anomaly... it’s been about two months. Yeah, roughly two months now. \n\nI remember exactly what was going on, too, because it coincided with the end of the fiscal quarter. I was taking on a few new high-net-worth individuals, really expanding my portfolio and having these highly confidential strategy sessions. And that’s when it started. The belief that people are tracking my client meetings and sending me signals has been going on for about two months, right from that specific point in time. \n\nBecause before that, maybe there was an odd coincidence here or there, but right around the eight-week mark, that’s when the frequency of it just spiked. I’d have a private consultation on a Tuesday about, say, tax-free municipal bonds, and by Thursday, someone at a downtown mixer would make a highly specific, pointed comment about that exact same financial vehicle while looking right at me. \n\nSo it’s been two solid months of this. Sixty days of constantly analyzing the overlap. It feels like a lifetime. I’ve even started color-coding my digital calendar to track the anomalies over this two-month period—red for a direct signal, yellow for a suspected one—and the concentration of it all is just overwhelming. It all started right after that big push for new clients, and it just hasn't let up for a single week since.\n\nDoctor: Did this start suddenly after a major stressful event?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I wouldn't call it sudden. And honestly, it wasn't really a stressful event that kicked it all off, either. I mean, not in a negative way, at least. If I really look at the whole picture—beyond just the last two months of the intense, absolute certainty I was just telling you about—these changes have actually been building since that arts nonprofit recognition a little over two years ago. \n\nI don't know if I mentioned the nonprofit stuff yet, but I do a fair amount of pro bono advisory work for some of the local galleries and theater groups here in the city. This gradual accumulation of oddities and subtle signals ever since that night two years ago. \n\nI can still picture the exact venue, standing by the bar and thinking, \"Why is everyone suddenly so intensely interested in my proprietary data?\" And it just grew from there, inch by inch, quarter by quarter. Well, I guess... I mean, "emotionally expressive" is a broad term, isn't it? But if you're asking about my motivation and my general energy levels, then yeah, there's definitely been a shift. I keep telling myself, \"Come on, it’s just a coincidence, Cincinnati isn't that big, it’s just how networking works.\" I try to brush it off. But I can’t. I just can’t let it go. It’s like this constant hum in the back of my mind, analyzing every interaction, every seating arrangement, every email subject line. It’s exhausting, honestly, trying to figure out what they’re trying to tell me or why they’re keeping tabs on me like this.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe for certain that these people are tracking you?\n\nPatient: Well, that's... that's the thing, isn't it? I mean, part of my brain, the logical part, the part that went to college and analyzes market trends and risk portfolios all day, that part says, \"Hey, Cincinnati isn't New York, right? It's a smaller pond. You're going to see the same fish.\" And I really do try to lean into that. I'll sit there at my desk, looking at an email invite to a gallery opening in Over-the-Rhine, and I'll see that the featured artist just happens to be doing a series on, I don't know, urban decay, which exactly mirrors a real estate development deal I was just discussing in private with a client the day before. But the feeling, the absolute conviction that they are keeping tabs on me, that they are coordinating these little signals to let me know they're watching my moves... it just overpowers the logic.
